newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN PUBLIC SECTOR INVESTMENT SEEN GROWING.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN PUBLIC SECTOR INVESTMENT SEEN GROWING.

text.p: The private sector-led fixed investment upswing of the last few years should be replaced by investment in public sector infrastructural projects over the next few years, Boland Bank economist Francois Jansen said on Thursday.
In his latest economic review, Jansen said the current investment cycle had started in March 1993. Since then, fixed investment had risen 30.5 percent while real GDP had risen by only 12.3 percent.

During that time private sector investment had risen 38.4 percent, mainly as a result of large projects such as Columbus and Alusaf, while that of public corporations had risen 25.5 percent and public authorities had shown no increase.
"Investment by public authorities is expected to gain momentum over the next few years as certain reconstruction and development programmes get off the ground," Jansen said.
"This type of investment will, for the most part, replace private sector investment over the next few years."

Much of the investment so far appeared to have been funded by capital inflows after a long period of net capital outflows. Jansen estimated that 28.1 billion rand had flowed into the country between April 1994 and the end of the third quarter of 1996
"Of this, more than 90 percent was of a long-term nature, of which it is hoped that a large proportion will find its way to physical investment," he said.

Provided that South Africa maintained a stable political environment and responsible economic policies, Jansen said the availability of capital for fixed investment should not be a problem for the coming year.

The low level of gross domestic savings, however, remained a concern. It now stood at 17 percent of GDP compared to more than 34.5 percent in 1980 and was preventing the economy from sustaining growth of more than 2.5 percent without incurring deficit.

Immediate prospects for a significant improvement in savings levels appeared limited. Although the state started cutting back on dissavings last year, it would take some time for this to contribute to the savings pool.
"By the same token, it will take time to boost the inclination and capacity of individuals to save," Jansen said.
The strong demand for credit also indicated that individuals savings were at very low levels.
